CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a bracket at a value that makes a denominator zero.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Solve the denominator-zero equation and exclude roots with open interval boundaries.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating an odd root as if it were an even root.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Odd roots accept negative real radicands.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Only even radicals demand a nonnegative radicand.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting domain alone when asked for range.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Range refers to attained output values, not permitted inputs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Study y-values using the function rule, not only its input restrictions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Connecting discrete annual observations with unproved continuous values.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Recorded points do not certify intermediate or extrapolated outputs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the observation domain separately from a supplied continuous model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying two piecewise branches to the same boundary input.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The inequalities allocate inputs between branches.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose the branch whose boundary condition actually contains the input.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a closed dot at an omitted piecewise endpoint.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A strict inequality excludes that endpoint.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Open circles mean excluded; filled circles mean included.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using an included branch boundary to assign two different values at the same x.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A piecewise function must have a single active formula at every permitted input.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Before evaluating a boundary, check exactly one inequality; a strict endpoint uses an open circle.

ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goals: determine domains for finite mappings and functions defined by formulas, convert unions and exclusions to interval and set-builder notation, read domain and range from graphs, and evaluate or graph piecewise functions.

Find the domain before computing outputs. For a polynomial every real input is permitted; for a rational function solve its denominator equal to zero and exclude those inputs; for an even root enforce a nonnegative radicand.
Parentheses exclude finite endpoints and brackets include them. Use ∪ to combine intervals and use a parenthesis with each infinite endpoint.

An isolated graph point contributes a specific input and output. A continuous curve contributes an interval of inputs and attained outputs. A source figure may be an observed data window, not proof about values outside it.

To determine range of a quadratic, identify its turning point and direction; to determine range of an odd-degree cubic with opposite end limits, recognize all real outputs; to determine range of a reciprocal, exclude any unattainable output.
A piecewise rule partitions inputs by strict or inclusive inequalities. Label open/closed circles and evaluate exactly one branch at a permitted input.

Context restricts mathematical domains: positive integer group sizes, a finite series of calendar years, real measurement units, or nonnegative flight height can exclude values that the algebra alone allows.

Teacher-led source-skill activity: compare domain and range on independent coordinate diagrams for reciprocal, radical, and multi-branch functions. Verify units, endpoint membership and graph axes manually.
Independent Try It practice contains eight independently authored tasks covering original Section 1.2 learner actions. Teachers assess graph constructions and open-ended reasoning.
Independent Try It 1 — Finite domain set. A mapping includes (−6,2),(0,5),(4,2),(9,8). Write its domain.
Independent Try It 2 — Polynomial domain. Find the real domain of F(x)=x⁵−2x²+4.
Independent Try It 3 — Rational restriction. Find the domain of f(x)=(3x+1)/(5x−4).
Independent Try It 4 — Root restriction. Find the domain of g(x)=√(3x+12).
Independent Try It 5 — Real interval descriptions. Write −3<x≤1 or x≥5 in interval notation.
Independent Try It 6 — Domain and range of a sampled function. At discrete years 2019,2020,2021,2022 the observed metric is 20,45,30,50. Give the observed input and output sets.
Independent Try It 7 — Radical range. For h(x)=−√(8−x), find real domain and range.
Independent Try It 8 — Piecewise with missing endpoints. Graph f(x)=x² if x<−1, f(x)=1 if −1<x<2 and f(x)=√(x−2) if x>2. State the domain and open endpoint behavior.

Independent Edulytics cool-down — (a) State the domain of f(x)=(x+1)/(x−2). (b) Give domain and range of g(x)=−√(9−x). (c) For h(x)=x+2 when x<0 and h(x)=x−1 when x≥0, evaluate h(0) and explain which point is closed. Submit separate rational-domain, radical-range and piecewise-endpoint explanations for teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain and range
KeyConcepts.Definition: The domain contains permitted input values and the range contains attained outputs.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read allowed x-values first; then identify all outputs actually attained.

KeyConcepts.Title: Interval notation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Parentheses omit finite endpoints and brackets include them.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Infinity is never included; unions combine disjoint allowed sets.

KeyConcepts.Title: Algebraic domain restriction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Polynomials accept all real inputs; rational denominators cannot vanish.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Even-root radicands must be nonnegative; root denominators must be strictly positive.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph-derived domain and range
KeyConcepts.Definition: Horizontal coverage yields domain, and vertical coverage yields range.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distinguish discrete points, continuous curves, open/closed endpoints and plotted windows.
KeyConcepts.Example: y=|x−1|−2 has all-real domain and range [−2,∞).

KeyConcepts.Title: Toolkit shapes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Quadratic ranges may be bounded below; cubic ranges cover ℝ; reciprocals omit a value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Analyze each exact rule and branch rather than assume a picture's drawn window is full domain.

KeyConcepts.Title: Piecewise functions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A piecewise function uses more than one formula on disjoint input conditions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: At each boundary apply only the permitted condition; annotate included and excluded endpoint points.
KeyConcepts.Example: f(x)=x² for x≤0 and f(x)=1 for x>0 gives f(0)=0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Applied domain and units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Real context can constrain otherwise unrestricted mathematical formulas.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Nonnegative quantities, integer counts, dates and physical units limit contextual domains.
KeyConcepts.Example: h(t)=−16t²+96t describes nonnegative height during t∈[0,6].

SummaryPoints: A domain is the complete set of permitted inputs, whereas the range consists of attained outputs.
Exclude zeros of rational denominators; include an even-root boundary when the radicand is zero unless it also lies in a denominator.
Use parentheses for omitted endpoints, brackets for included endpoints, and unions for separated intervals.
A graph's input and output extents can be discrete, bounded or unbounded.
For piecewise rules select one branch by its inequality and mark open or filled endpoints.
Use physical contexts and units to narrow an algebraically permitted domain.
Independent open-ended graph reasoning is teacher-assessed, not automatically graded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Finite domain of a tabulated relation
WorkedExamples.Question: A function has the finite pairs {(1,11),(3,11),(5,15),(8,20)}. List its domain as a set.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: Keep only first coordinates, since inputs define the domain.
Remove duplicates without changing the input values.
WorkedExamples.Check: The repeated output 11 does not change the domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: All-real polynomial domain
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the domain of the polynomial F(x)=2x³−x+7 in interval notation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: Powers with whole-number exponents exist at every real input.
No denominator or even radical restricts x.
WorkedExamples.Check: Substitute any real number; the polynomial is defined.

WorkedExamples.Title: Domain excluding a denominator zero
WorkedExamples.Question: Determine the real domain of R(x)=(x+4)/(x−3).
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: Solve the forbidden denominator condition x−3=0.
Remove 3 from the real line and use an open endpoint on both sides.

WorkedExamples.Title: Domain of an even root
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the domain of S(x)=√(11−2x).
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: Enforce 11−2x≥0.
Solve −2x≥−11, reversing the inequality when dividing by a negative.
WorkedExamples.Check: The endpoint x=11/2 gives zero and is included.

WorkedExamples.Title: Open and closed interval unions
WorkedExamples.Question: Describe the independent real set −1≤x≤2 or x>4 using set-builder and interval notation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: The first component includes both −1 and 2.
The second component excludes 4 and has no finite upper endpoint.
WorkedExamples.Check: Brackets include, parentheses exclude; infinity always uses a parenthesis.

WorkedExamples.Title: Finite graph domain and range with open and closed endpoints
WorkedExamples.Question: An independent parabola segment follows f(x)=(x+1)²−4 only for −3<x≤1. Plot it with correct open/filled boundary points and find its domain and range.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated function restriction for domain and the vertex and attained endpoints for range.
Steps: The x-window is −3<x≤1, so the domain is (−3,1].
The left endpoint would be (−3,0), but it is OPEN because x=−3 is excluded.
The vertex (−1,−4) is included and gives the smallest output.
The right endpoint (1,0) is included, so 0 is in the range despite the excluded left endpoint.
WorkedExamples.Check: An excluded endpoint may still have an attained y-value elsewhere; range inclusion requires checking ALL graphed points.

WorkedExamples.Title: Observed continuous interpolation has a bounded domain and range
WorkedExamples.Question: A first-party environmental metric is recorded in tons/day for 2018–2023: 120,150,180,130,220,200. Model a CHART by connecting consecutive annual points with straight line segments. Read the domain and range of the displayed interpolation, and distinguish them from data outside the window.
WorkedExamples.Method: The sampled annual values are given; a continuous interpolation is explicitly defined only between sampled years.
Steps: Label x as year (2018–2023) and y as metric (tons/day); connect consecutive points only inside that closed window.
Under the explicitly specified piecewise-linear interpolation, every time t from 2018 to 2023 has one output.
The observed and interpolated minimum is 120 and maximum is 220 tons/day.
Do not infer that the actual process has those bounds before 2018 or after 2023.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Displayed interpolation: domain [2018,2023] years; range [120,220] tons/day.
WorkedExamples.Check: Units and the measurement window are essential; unobserved years are not automatically in the domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Domain and range of a cubic
WorkedExamples.Question: Find domain and range of f(x)=x³−4x.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: The polynomial is defined for all real x.
As x→∞ the cubic grows without bound; as x→−∞ it decreases without bound.
WorkedExamples.Check: Continuity and unbounded opposite end behavior yield every real output.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reciprocal domain and range
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=4/(x−2), find the real domain and range.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: The denominator x−2 cannot equal zero, so x≠2.
Because the numerator is nonzero, the output cannot equal zero; every other real y occurs for x=2+4/y.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check x=2 undefined and f(x)=0 impossible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Radical domain and range
WorkedExamples.Question: Find domain and range of f(x)=3√(x+1).
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: Require x+1≥0, so x≥−1.
The principal square root is nonnegative, so multiplying by 3 preserves outputs y≥0.
WorkedExamples.Check: At x=−1 the value is zero and larger inputs yield arbitrarily large outputs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct an integer-input piecewise cost rule
WorkedExamples.Question: A tour costs $6 per participant for groups of 1–7 and a flat $48 for groups of 8 or more. Write C(n).
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: People counts n must be positive integers.
For 1≤n≤7, use C(n)=6n.
For n≥8, use C(n)=48.
WorkedExamples.Answer: C(n)=6n for integers 1≤n≤7; C(n)=48 for integers n≥8.
WorkedExamples.Check: C(7)=42; C(8)=48. The real-line curve must not imply fractional people.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate two piecewise pricing intervals
WorkedExamples.Question: Let P(g)=20 for 0<g<3 and P(g)=20+8(g−3) for g≥3. Find P(2) and P(5).
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
WorkedExamples.Check: At g=3 the second branch applies and gives 20.

WorkedExamples.Title: Graph a three-piece definition with endpoints
WorkedExamples.Question: Let f(x)=x² for x≤0, f(x)=2 for 0<x≤3, and f(x)=x−1 for x>3. Identify open and closed endpoints, domain, and whether the graph is a function.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify inputs, mathematical restrictions, endpoint inclusions and output values.
Steps: At x=0 use the quadratic branch, with filled (0,0) and open (0,2).
At x=3 use the constant branch, with filled (3,2); the last segment begins just right of 3.
Each x belongs to exactly one branch, and the combined domain covers every real x.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Domain (−∞,∞); the graph is a function. At x=0, f(0)=0; at x=3, f(3)=2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Open and closed dots distinguish which branch includes each boundary.
